$$e_i=I^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes U(q)\otimes I^{\otimes(L-i-1)},\quad 1\le i<L,$$
where
$$U(q)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\0&q^{-1}&-1&0\\0&-1&q&0\\0&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}=-\frac12\bigl(X\otimes X+Y\otimes Y+\cos\gamma\,Z\otimes Z-\cos\gamma\,I_4+i\sin\gamma\,(Z\otimes I_2-I_2\otimes Z)\bigr).$$
The open-chain Temperley–Lieb Hamiltonian convention is $H_L=-\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}e_i$. No wrap-around term couples site $L$ to site $1$. This defines local operators; the following result proves their Temperley–Lieb relations.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. Let $I_n$ be the two-sided ideal generated by

$$u_i^2-\delta u_i\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad u_i u_j-u_j u_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$

and

$$u_i u_{i+1}u_i-u_i,\qquad u_{i+1}u_i u_{i+1}-u_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2).$$

The abstract **rank-$n$ Temperley–Lieb algebra** is the presented $R$-algebra

$$P_n(R,\delta):=F_n/I_n.$$

V_{n+1,b}\!\downarrow_{K_n}\cong\bigoplus_{\substack{0\le a\le\ell-2\\|a-b|=1}}V_{n,a},
$$
with each summand occurring once; vertices outside $\{0,\ldots,\ell-2\}$ contribute no summand.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. Define the quantum integers by

$$[0]_\delta=0,\qquad [1]_\delta=1,\qquad [r+1]_\delta=\delta[r]_\delta-[r-1]_\delta\quad(r\ge1).$$

The **quantum characteristic** of $(R,\delta)$ is the least positive integer $\ell$ with $[\ell]_\delta=0$, if one exists, and $\ell=\infty$ otherwise. No element of $R$ is inverted in this definition.

For $q\in\mathbb C^\times$ and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, write $[r]_q=[r]_\delta$. If $q\ne\pm1$, this agrees with $(q^r-q^{-r})/(q-q^{-1})$; at $q=\pm1$ the recurrence gives $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}$. For complex-parameter classification, write $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$, with $\kappa=\infty$ when $q^2$ has infinite order. If $q\ne\pm1$, the quantum characteristic equals $\kappa$ when $\kappa<\infty$ and is $\infty$ otherwise. At $q=\pm1$, $\kappa=1$ but the complex quantum characteristic is $\infty$, because $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}\ne0$ for every positive $r$.

For a field $K$ of positive characteristic $p$, set $p(0)=1$ and, when $\ell<\infty$, set $p(i)=\ell p^{i-1}$ for $i\ge1$. In characteristic zero and finite $\ell$, the finite digit scale is $p(1)=\ell$; the separate characteristic-zero criterion below uses $a\ell-1$ for arbitrary positive integers $a$. If $\ell=\infty$, every finite index is already in the range $n<\ell$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $n\ge1$, $\delta\in\mathbb C^\times$, and let $\iota_n,E_n$ be as in [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-tower-and-right-closure]]. Then $\iota_n$ is an injective unital algebra homomorphism, $E_n\iota_n=\mathrm{id}$, and for $a,b\in\mathrm{TL}_n$ and $x\in\mathrm{TL}_{n+1}$,
$$
E_n(\iota_n(a)x\iota_n(b))=aE_n(x)b,\qquad \tau_n(E_n(x))=\tau_{n+1}(x).
$$
If $d_n$ is the elementary cup-cap generator on the last two strands, then
$$
E_n(\iota_n(x)d_n)=\delta^{-1}x,\qquad \tau_{n+1}(\iota_n(x)d_n)=\delta^{-1}\tau_n(x).
$$
When $\delta\in\mathbb R$, $\iota_n$ also preserves the reflection involution. Moreover, if $\delta\in\mathbb R^\times$, the involution is compatible with finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebra structures on the tower and the Markov traces are faithful positive traces, then $E_n$ is positive and hence is a positive trace-preserving conditional expectation.

Let $n\ge1$ and $\delta\in\mathbb C^\times$. Define the trace-pairing radical
$$
J_n:=\{x\in\mathrm{TL}_n(\mathbb C,\delta):\tau_n(yx)=0\text{ for every }y\in\mathrm{TL}_n(\mathbb C,\delta)\}.
$$
Then $J_n$ is a two-sided ideal, $\iota_n(J_n)\subseteq J_{n+1}$, and $E_n(J_{n+1})\subseteq J_n$. Consequently the inclusion and normalized right closure descend to the quotient tower $\mathrm{TL}_n/J_n$.

Starting with $p_0=p_1=1$, induction in the JW recursion shows $p_r^*=p_r$ through $r=\ell-1$: reflection fixes $P_r=p_r\otimes1$ and $U_r$, while the coefficient $[r]/[r+1]$ is real whenever this recursion is used. In particular the boundary projector $p_{\ell-1}$ is self-adjoint. For $n<\ell-1$, the generated ideal component $I_n$ is zero and is reflection-stable; for $n\ge\ell-1$, its fixed embedded generator $p_{\ell-1}\otimes1$ is self-adjoint, so $I_n=\mathrm{TL}_n(p_{\ell-1}\otimes1)\mathrm{TL}_n$ is reflection-stable because $(x(p_{\ell-1}\otimes1)y)^*=y^*(p_{\ell-1}\otimes1)x^*$. By [F3], these are the endomorphism components of the generated negligible tensor ideal. Also [F7] gives $\tau_n(D^*)=\overline{\tau_n(D)}$ on diagrams and hence on all elements. Fix a retained endpoint $1\le a\le k$, write $f_a=p_a\otimes1$, and use the supplier's maps $\alpha_a=f_a(1_{a-1}\otimes\mathrm{cup})p_{a-1}$ and $\beta_a=p_{a-1}(1_{a-1}\otimes\mathrm{cap})f_a$. Horizontal reflection reverses composition and exchanges the cup and cap; step 1.1 fixes $f_a$ and $p_{a-1}$, so $\alpha_a^*=\beta_a$. The supplier identity $\beta_a\alpha_a=\lambda_a p_{a-1}$ therefore gives $\alpha_a^*\alpha_a=\lambda_a p_{a-1}$. Set $v_a=\lambda_a^{-1/2}\alpha_a$. Then $v_a^*v_a=p_{a-1}$ and $v_av_a^*=\lambda_a^{-1}\alpha_a\beta_a$, the down projection in the JW split. For $a<k$, the complementary up projection is $p_{a+1}$; it is self-adjoint by step 1.1 and orthogonal to the down projection by the JW turnback relations in [F2]. At $a=k$, the quotient kills $p_{k+1}=p_{\ell-1}$ before normalization, so only the down projection remains. The up inclusion and retraction are adjoints, as are $v_a$ and $v_a^*$. Composing these isometric branch maps along retained paths gives path maps $I_p$ with mutually orthogonal ranges and $\sum_p I_pI_p^*=1_n$. Hence $F_{p,q}=I_pI_q^*$ are complete matrix units and $F_{p,q}^*=F_{q,p}$. Their diagonal units equal the supplier's path projections (the reciprocal branch normalizations cancel), so $\operatorname{Tr}_n(F_{p,q})=\delta_{p,q}[a+1]$ by [F2]. Thus the quotient with its inherited reflection is a direct sum of full complex matrix algebras with the usual adjoint, hence a finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebra. Since $\tau_n(F_{p,p})=\delta^{-n}[a+1]>0$, its normalized closure trace is faithful positive.

Tensoring an endpoint path map with a strand and resolving its endpoint identity by the same isometric up/down splitting gives $F_{p,q}\otimes1=\sum_c F_{pc,qc}$. The coefficients are exactly one because the inclusion and retraction at each common endpoint use reciprocal normalizations. At $a=k$ delete $p_{k+1}$ before splitting; only its down term remains, as in [F2]. Thus the actual quotient inclusions are exactly the prefix maps of [F4]; no compatibility is imposed as an additional hypothesis. Transporting the endpoint action along these matrix units and applying [F4] gives the asserted multiplicity-one branching, omitting zero path spaces and invalid boundary labels.

[F1] defines $\bar\iota_n([x])=[\iota_n(x)]$ and $\bar E_n([z])=[E_n(z)]$ independently of representatives. Bimodularity, trace preservation and $\bar E_n\bar\iota_n=\mathrm{id}$ pass to these quotients, so inclusion is injective. Its compatibility with reflection follows from real $\delta$. Closure also commutes with reflection: the two finite matching graphs obtained by reflecting before or after closing have the same components and the real factor $\delta^{-1}$. Thus $\bar E_n$ is star-preserving. For $z\ge0$ and $b\in Q_n$, bimodularity gives $\tau_n(b^*\bar E_n(z)b)=\tau_{n+1}(\bar\iota_n(b)^*z\bar\iota_n(b))\ge0$. Bimodularity with the endpoint central projections shows that $\bar E_n(F_{pc,qc})=0$ if the predecessor endpoints $a,b$ differ. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal B(H)$ denote
its bounded linear operators. Applying AC to a family indexed by the natural numbers
supplies Countable Choice, the hypothesis of
[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]], which provides adjoints on $\mathcal B(H)$.
A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a
unital $*$-subalgebra $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ that is closed in the
weak operator topology (WOT). Here unital means $I_H\in\mathcal A$; the zero
Hilbert space is allowed, with $I_H=0$ and sole unital algebra $\{0\}$. This is
the only use of AC in this definition.

For any set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, its **commutant** and
**double commutant** are
$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):TS=ST\text{ for every }S\in\mathcal S\},\qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$
Commutants are taken inside $\mathcal B(H)$. The **von Neumann algebra
generated by $\mathcal S$** is
$$W^*(\mathcal S):=\overline{\operatorname{Alg}^*(\mathcal S\cup\{I_H\})}^{\,\mathrm{WOT}},$$
the WOT closure in $\mathcal B(H)$ of the unital $*$-algebra generated by
$\mathcal S$. No bicommutant theorem is part of these definitions.

Two elementary properties will be used. For fixed $S\in\mathcal B(H)$,
$$\langle TS\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T(S\xi),\eta\rangle,\qquad \langle ST\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T\xi,S^*\eta\rangle$$
are WOT-continuous matrix coefficients as functions of $T$. Thus each equation
$TS=ST$ defines a WOT-closed set, and so $\mathcal S'$ is WOT-closed. If
$\mathcal S$ is self-adjoint, then $\mathcal S'$ is a unital $*$-subalgebra:
products preserve commutation with every $S$, and taking adjoints of $TS=ST$
gives $ST^*=T^*S$. These facts do not identify $W^*(\mathcal S)$ with
$\mathcal S''$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). A complex-linear functional $\tau:M\to\mathbb C$ is **positive** if $\tau(P)\in[0,+\infty)$ for every positive operator $P\in M$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]), a **state** if it is positive and $\tau(I_H)=1$, **normal** if its restriction to the operator-norm unit ball of $M$ is continuous for the relative weak-operator topology ([[def-strong-and-weak-operator-topologies]], [[def-operator-norm]]), **tracial** if $\tau(ST)=\tau(TS)$ for all $S,T\in M$, and **faithful** if $\tau(T^*T)=0$ implies $T=0$. A **faithful normal tracial state** is a positive normalized trace that is both normal and faithful. In particular, $(M,\tau)$ is a **finite tracial von Neumann algebra** when $\tau$ is a faithful normal tracial state. If $H=\{0\}$ then $M=\{0\}$ and has no state, since $I_H=0$.

For a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $K$, the normalized matrix trace $\operatorname{tr}_K/\dim K$ is a faithful normal tracial state on $\mathcal B(K)$, and it is the unique tracial state.

For a discrete group $\Gamma$ equipped with the discrete topology, let $H_\Gamma=\ell^2(\Gamma,\mathbb C)$, whose Hilbert-space structure under AC is established in the proof. Define the left and right regular operators by
$$
(\lambda_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(g^{-1}h),\qquad (\rho_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(hg)\qquad(g,h\in\Gamma).
$$
Put $L(\Gamma):=W^*(\lambda_\Gamma(\Gamma))$ using the concrete generated von Neumann algebra of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]]. Then
$$
\tau_\Gamma(T):=\langle T\delta_e,\delta_e\rangle\qquad(T\in L(\Gamma))
$$
is a faithful normal tracial state on $L(\Gamma)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital $*$-subalgebra closed in the weak operator topology. Then $M''=M$, and $M$ is also closed in the strong operator topology. Consequently the concrete von Neumann algebras of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]] are exactly the unital $*$-subalgebras that are closed in either of these topologies. For an arbitrary set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ one has $W^*(\mathcal S)''=W^*(\mathcal S)$.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$D\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a nondegenerate concrete C*-algebra
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]],
[[def-c-star-algebra]], [[def-nondegenerate-star-representation-of-a-banach-star-algebra]]).
Set $M:=D''$ in the commutant convention of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]]. If $H=\{0\}$, the operator-density and transitivity clauses below
are trivial; assume $H\ne\{0\}$ for those clauses. Then:

1. $D_{\mathrm{sa}}$ is strongly dense in $M_{\mathrm{sa}}$, and the unit ball
   of $D$ is strongly dense in the unit ball of $M$.
2. If $M=\mathcal B(H)$, then every finite self-adjoint vector prescription
   compatible with a self-adjoint operator is realized exactly: for
   $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\in H$ and $c=c^*\in\mathcal B(H)$, there is
   $a=a^*\in D$ with $a\xi_j=c\xi_j$ for all $j$. Separately, if the prescribed vectors are finitely many orthonormal
   eigenvectors of $c$ with eigenvalues in a closed interval
   $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ containing $0$, an $a\in D_{\mathrm{sa}}$ can be
   chosen with spectrum in $J$ and the same eigenvalues on those vectors.
   This spectrum-constrained variant makes no promise about additional
   arbitrary vector prescriptions after clipping.
3. If $M=\mathcal B(H)$, then for any unit vectors $\xi,\eta\in H$ there is a unitary $u$ in the
   minimal unitization $D^\sim$ ([[thm-minimal-c-star-unitization]]) whose
   represented operator sends $\xi$ to $z\eta$ for some $z\in\mathbb C$ with
   $|z|=1$. Here unitary has the usual C*-algebra meaning
   ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-elements-of-a-c-star-algebra]]),
   and $D^\sim=D$ when $D$ is unital and $D+\mathbb C I$ otherwise.

For a complex C*-algebra $A$, two pure states $\phi,\psi$ are called unitarily
equivalent here when $\psi=\phi\circ\operatorname{Ad}(u)$ for some unitary
$u\in U(A^\sim)$, where $\operatorname{Ad}(u)(a)=uau^*$ and $A^\sim=A$ when
$A$ is unital and its minimal unitization otherwise
([[thm-minimal-c-star-unitization]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-elements-of-a-c-star-algebra]]). Their GNS
representations are irreducible exactly when the states are pure
([[lem-c-star-state-gns-purity-and-polish-state-space]],
[[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]]). If their GNS representations are
inequivalent, then $\|\phi-\psi\|=2$. Orthogonal unit vectors in one
irreducible carrier likewise give vector states at distance $2$. Consequently,
if $\|\phi-\psi\|<2$, then $\phi$ and $\psi$ are unitarily equivalent.

**Assume the ultrafilter lemma.**  If $X$ is a real or complex normed space,
then its closed dual unit ball $B_{X^*}$ is compact in the weak-star topology
$\sigma(X^*,X)$.  Completeness of $X$ is not required.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a complex normed space, let $M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, and
let $f_0:M \to \mathbb{C}$ be a bounded complex linear functional. Then there
exists a bounded complex linear functional $F:X \to \mathbb{C}$ such that
$F|_M=f_0$ and $\|F\|=\|f_0\|$.

Assume HB. Let $A,B$ be disjoint nonempty convex subsets of a real or complex normed space $X$.

(i) If $A$ is open, there are $0\ne f\in X^*$ and $a\in\mathbb R$ with
$$\operatorname{Re}f(x)<a\le\operatorname{Re}f(y)\qquad(x\in A,\ y\in B).$$
If $B$ is also open, the right inequality is strict too. If only $B$ is open, interchange the labels and negate the functional to put the strict inequality on the $B$ side.

(ii) If $A$ is closed and $B$ is compact, there are $0\ne f\in X^*$, $a\in\mathbb R$, and $\varepsilon>0$ with
$$\operatorname{Re}f(x)\le a-\varepsilon<a+\varepsilon\le\operatorname{Re}f(y)\qquad(x\in A,\ y\in B).$$
In particular, a point outside a nonempty closed convex set is uniformly strictly separated from it. All inequalities concern real parts.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert
space $H$, let $E$ be its spectral projection valued measure on $\sigma(T)$, and
let $f\mapsto f(T)$ be the bounded Borel functional calculus of
[[def-borel-functional-calculus-for-a-bounded-normal-operator]]. Then:

1. $f(T)$ extends the continuous calculus: for continuous $f$ it agrees with
   the operator denoted $f(T)$ by
   [[thm-continuous-functional-calculus-for-bounded-normal-operators]], and
   $\mathbf 1_B(T)=E(B)$ for every Borel $B\subseteq\sigma(T)$;
2. the calculus is linear, unital, multiplicative and star-preserving:
   $(af+bg)(T)=af(T)+bg(T)$, $\mathbf 1(T)=I$, $(fg)(T)=f(T)g(T)$ and
   $\overline f(T)=f(T)^*$;
3. $\|f(T)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x$ for every $x\in H$ and
   $\|f(T)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty}\le\|f\|_\infty$, the exact norm being the
   $E$-essential supremum of $f$; in particular $f(T)$ is normal with
   $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
4. if $(f_n)$ are uniformly bounded Borel functions, $f$ is bounded Borel, and
   $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere, then $f_n(T)\to f(T)$ in the
   strong operator topology;
5. every $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ commuting with $T$ and $T^*$ commutes with every
   $f(T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

derivations.claim: We use the repository convention that scalar Hilbert inner products are linear in their first variable. Right-module-valued inner products, introduced later, are conjugate-linear in the first variable as usual.

**Standard commutants.** Right multiplication satisfies $\|ax\|_2\le \|x\| \|a\|_2$, and left multiplication has the analogous estimate. Their ranges are von Neumann algebras: for example the unit ball of $L(A)$ is strongly closed: the unit ball of $A$ is WOT compact. To obtain this directly without a predual assumption, apply Banach–Alaoglu to the unit ball of $B(K)$ as bounded sesquilinear forms on its original carrier $K$; $A$ is WOT closed. Every standard-representation coefficient $a\mapsto t(b^*ac)$ is normal and therefore WOT continuous on this ball; arbitrary $L^2$ coefficients follow uniformly by approximating both vectors by $A$. Thus the image ball of $L(A)$ is WOT compact and hence strongly closed. The representation is faithful and isometric (the norm can be detected by nonzero spectral projections of $a^*a$). Its range is a norm-closed unital C*-algebra. The published bounded-density supplier, applied to this range and its bicommutant, now promotes closedness of its unit ball to $L(A)=L(A)''$, so the whole range is a von Neumann algebra. This avoids the invalid inference that every strongly convergent net is uniformly bounded. The coefficient calculation directly proves WOT continuity on bounded balls, so the representation is normal in the stated convention. Let $LC$ be the bounded operators $L_\xi :a\mapsto \xi a$ associated with vectors $\xi \in L^2(A)$, and let $RC$ be the analogous right convolvers. These operators commute with each other. Here is the limit argument, to avoid assuming that bounded vectors belong to $A$: choose $a_n\to \xi $, $b_m\to \eta $ in $L^2$ with $a_n,b_m\in A$. For fixed $c,d\in A$, the coefficients of $a_n c b_m$ have a joint limit, because the trace identity writes them explicitly as $\langle a_n c b_m,d\rangle =\langle c b_m,a_n^* d\rangle $, an inner product of two convergent Hilbert sequences, where $J(a)=a^*$. Taking first the $n$ limit or first the $m$ limit therefore gives the same result. If $L_\xi $ and $R_\eta $ are bounded, the two iterated limits are respectively the coefficients of $L_\xi R_\eta (c)$ and $R_\eta L_\xi (c)$. Density of $A$ proves commutation.

If $T\in R(A)'$, set $\xi =T1$. On $A$, $T(a)=T(R_a1)=R_a\xi =\xi a$, so $T=L_\xi $. Thus $LC=R(A)'$; similarly $RC=L(A)'$. The preceding commutation gives $LC\subseteq RC'=L(A)''=L(A)$ by the bicommutant theorem. The reverse inclusion is immediate. This proves both commutant identities and the bounded-vector criterion. Notice that sequences approximate individual Hilbert vectors regardless of whether $L^2(A)$ is separable.

**Positive-vector realization; no unproved Radon–Nikodym input.** Here are functional analytic details underlying the normal-functional approximation used next. For a concrete von Neumann algebra $Q\subseteq B(K)$, its normal functionals form the quotient of the trace-class operators on $K$ by the annihilator of $Q$, with dual $Q$. Here is the pairing and duality in detail. For finite-rank $h$, use its finite-dimensional trace to define the pairing $\operatorname{Tr}(hx)$. If $h=\sum_j\langle\,\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j$, it equals $\sum_j\langle xv_j,u_j\rangle$, so its modulus is at most $\|x\|\|h\|_1$ by taking the infimum over nuclear representations. Finite-rank density [F11] extends this pairing to all trace-class $h$. Conversely a bounded functional on trace class, evaluated at the rank-one operators, gives a bounded sesquilinear form on $K$; [F7] represents it by a unique $x\in B(K)$. Equality of the functional and this pairing on finite-rank operators extends by trace-norm density, and testing rank-one operators proves equality of norms. Thus the dual of trace class is $B(K)$. The dual of its quotient by the annihilator of $Q$ is the double annihilator, which is $Q$ because $Q$ is ultraweakly closed. The double-annihilator assertion follows by applying Hahn–Banach separation to a point outside the closed linear space. A WOT-closed linear space is ultraweakly closed. For completeness, the stipulated bounded-ball WOT continuity gives approximation in norm by finite matrix coefficients. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal B(H)$ denote
its bounded linear operators. Applying AC to a family indexed by the natural numbers
supplies Countable Choice, the hypothesis of
[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]], which provides adjoints on $\mathcal B(H)$.
A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a
unital $*$-subalgebra $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ that is closed in the
weak operator topology (WOT). Here unital means $I_H\in\mathcal A$; the zero
Hilbert space is allowed, with $I_H=0$ and sole unital algebra $\{0\}$. This is
the only use of AC in this definition.

For any set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, its **commutant** and
**double commutant** are
$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):TS=ST\text{ for every }S\in\mathcal S\},\qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$
Commutants are taken inside $\mathcal B(H)$. The **von Neumann algebra
generated by $\mathcal S$** is
$$W^*(\mathcal S):=\overline{\operatorname{Alg}^*(\mathcal S\cup\{I_H\})}^{\,\mathrm{WOT}},$$
the WOT closure in $\mathcal B(H)$ of the unital $*$-algebra generated by
$\mathcal S$. No bicommutant theorem is part of these definitions.

Two elementary properties will be used. For fixed $S\in\mathcal B(H)$,
$$\langle TS\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T(S\xi),\eta\rangle,\qquad \langle ST\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T\xi,S^*\eta\rangle$$
are WOT-continuous matrix coefficients as functions of $T$. Thus each equation
$TS=ST$ defines a WOT-closed set, and so $\mathcal S'$ is WOT-closed. If
$\mathcal S$ is self-adjoint, then $\mathcal S'$ is a unital $*$-subalgebra:
products preserve commutation with every $S$, and taking adjoints of $TS=ST$
gives $ST^*=T^*S$. These facts do not identify $W^*(\mathcal S)$ with
$\mathcal S''$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). A complex-linear functional $\tau:M\to\mathbb C$ is **positive** if $\tau(P)\in[0,+\infty)$ for every positive operator $P\in M$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]), a **state** if it is positive and $\tau(I_H)=1$, **normal** if its restriction to the operator-norm unit ball of $M$ is continuous for the relative weak-operator topology ([[def-strong-and-weak-operator-topologies]], [[def-operator-norm]]), **tracial** if $\tau(ST)=\tau(TS)$ for all $S,T\in M$, and **faithful** if $\tau(T^*T)=0$ implies $T=0$. A **faithful normal tracial state** is a positive normalized trace that is both normal and faithful. In particular, $(M,\tau)$ is a **finite tracial von Neumann algebra** when $\tau$ is a faithful normal tracial state. If $H=\{0\}$ then $M=\{0\}$ and has no state, since $I_H=0$.

For a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $K$, the normalized matrix trace $\operatorname{tr}_K/\dim K$ is a faithful normal tracial state on $\mathcal B(K)$, and it is the unique tracial state.

For a discrete group $\Gamma$ equipped with the discrete topology, let $H_\Gamma=\ell^2(\Gamma,\mathbb C)$, whose Hilbert-space structure under AC is established in the proof. Define the left and right regular operators by
$$
(\lambda_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(g^{-1}h),\qquad (\rho_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(hg)\qquad(g,h\in\Gamma).
$$
Put $L(\Gamma):=W^*(\lambda_\Gamma(\Gamma))$ using the concrete generated von Neumann algebra of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]]. Then
$$
\tau_\Gamma(T):=\langle T\delta_e,\delta_e\rangle\qquad(T\in L(\Gamma))
$$
is a faithful normal tracial state on $L(\Gamma)$.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ a concrete von Neumann algebra
([[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]]). If $H=\{0\}$, part 1 is the
trivial zero-operator decomposition and part 2 has no nonzero projection inputs;
assume $H\ne\{0\}$ for the remaining clauses. A projection means a self-adjoint
idempotent in $M$; for projections $r,p$, $r\le p$ means $rp=pr=r$.
Projections $r,s\in M$ are called equivalent when there is a partial isometry
$w\in M$ with $w^*w=r$ and $ww^*=s$. Write $pMq:=\{pmq:m\in M\}$. Then:

1. Every $x\in M$ has a polar decomposition $x=v|x|$, where
   $|x|:=(x^*x)^{1/2}\in M$ and $v\in M$ is a partial isometry
   ([[def-isometry-coisometry-and-partial-isometry]]) with $v^*v$ the
   orthogonal projection onto $(\ker x)^\perp$ and $vv^*$ the orthogonal
   projection onto $\overline{\operatorname{ran}x}$.
2. If $M$ is a factor, meaning $M\cap M'=\mathbb C I$, and $p,q\in M$ are
   nonzero projections, then $pMq\ne\{0\}$. In particular, a nonzero partial
   isometry $v\in M$ exists with $v^*v\le p$ and $vv^*\le q$; equivalently,
   a nonzero subprojection of $p$ is equivalent to a nonzero subprojection of
   $q$.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert
space $H$, let $E$ be its spectral projection valued measure on $\sigma(T)$, and
let $f\mapsto f(T)$ be the bounded Borel functional calculus of
[[def-borel-functional-calculus-for-a-bounded-normal-operator]]. Then:

1. $f(T)$ extends the continuous calculus: for continuous $f$ it agrees with
   the operator denoted $f(T)$ by
   [[thm-continuous-functional-calculus-for-bounded-normal-operators]], and
   $\mathbf 1_B(T)=E(B)$ for every Borel $B\subseteq\sigma(T)$;
2. the calculus is linear, unital, multiplicative and star-preserving:
   $(af+bg)(T)=af(T)+bg(T)$, $\mathbf 1(T)=I$, $(fg)(T)=f(T)g(T)$ and
   $\overline f(T)=f(T)^*$;
3. $\|f(T)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x$ for every $x\in H$ and
   $\|f(T)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty}\le\|f\|_\infty$, the exact norm being the
   $E$-essential supremum of $f$; in particular $f(T)$ is normal with
   $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
4. if $(f_n)$ are uniformly bounded Borel functions, $f$ is bounded Borel, and
   $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere, then $f_n(T)\to f(T)$ in the
   strong operator topology;
5. every $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ commuting with $T$ and $T^*$ commutes with every
   $f(T)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal B(H)$ denote
its bounded linear operators. Applying AC to a family indexed by the natural numbers
supplies Countable Choice, the hypothesis of
[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]], which provides adjoints on $\mathcal B(H)$.
A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a
unital $*$-subalgebra $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ that is closed in the
weak operator topology (WOT). Here unital means $I_H\in\mathcal A$; the zero
Hilbert space is allowed, with $I_H=0$ and sole unital algebra $\{0\}$. This is
the only use of AC in this definition.

For any set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, its **commutant** and
**double commutant** are
$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):TS=ST\text{ for every }S\in\mathcal S\},\qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$
Commutants are taken inside $\mathcal B(H)$. The **von Neumann algebra
generated by $\mathcal S$** is
$$W^*(\mathcal S):=\overline{\operatorname{Alg}^*(\mathcal S\cup\{I_H\})}^{\,\mathrm{WOT}},$$
the WOT closure in $\mathcal B(H)$ of the unital $*$-algebra generated by
$\mathcal S$. No bicommutant theorem is part of these definitions.

Two elementary properties will be used. For fixed $S\in\mathcal B(H)$,
$$\langle TS\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T(S\xi),\eta\rangle,\qquad \langle ST\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T\xi,S^*\eta\rangle$$
are WOT-continuous matrix coefficients as functions of $T$. Thus each equation
$TS=ST$ defines a WOT-closed set, and so $\mathcal S'$ is WOT-closed. If
$\mathcal S$ is self-adjoint, then $\mathcal S'$ is a unital $*$-subalgebra:
products preserve commutation with every $S$, and taking adjoints of $TS=ST$
gives $ST^*=T^*S$. These facts do not identify $W^*(\mathcal S)$ with
$\mathcal S''$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). A complex-linear functional $\tau:M\to\mathbb C$ is **positive** if $\tau(P)\in[0,+\infty)$ for every positive operator $P\in M$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]), a **state** if it is positive and $\tau(I_H)=1$, **normal** if its restriction to the operator-norm unit ball of $M$ is continuous for the relative weak-operator topology ([[def-strong-and-weak-operator-topologies]], [[def-operator-norm]]), **tracial** if $\tau(ST)=\tau(TS)$ for all $S,T\in M$, and **faithful** if $\tau(T^*T)=0$ implies $T=0$. A **faithful normal tracial state** is a positive normalized trace that is both normal and faithful. In particular, $(M,\tau)$ is a **finite tracial von Neumann algebra** when $\tau$ is a faithful normal tracial state. If $H=\{0\}$ then $M=\{0\}$ and has no state, since $I_H=0$.

For a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $K$, the normalized matrix trace $\operatorname{tr}_K/\dim K$ is a faithful normal tracial state on $\mathcal B(K)$, and it is the unique tracial state.

For a discrete group $\Gamma$ equipped with the discrete topology, let $H_\Gamma=\ell^2(\Gamma,\mathbb C)$, whose Hilbert-space structure under AC is established in the proof. Define the left and right regular operators by
$$
(\lambda_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(g^{-1}h),\qquad (\rho_\Gamma(g)f)(h)=f(hg)\qquad(g,h\in\Gamma).
$$
Put $L(\Gamma):=W^*(\lambda_\Gamma(\Gamma))$ using the concrete generated von Neumann algebra of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]]. Then
$$
\tau_\Gamma(T):=\langle T\delta_e,\delta_e\rangle\qquad(T\in L(\Gamma))
$$
is a faithful normal tracial state on $L(\Gamma)$.

Assume AC. Here normality for positive functionals and positive maps means WOT continuity on every operator-norm bounded ball, agreeing with the published trace convention. For a finite tracial von Neumann algebra $(A,t)$, left and right multiplication
on $L^2(A,t)$ are faithful normal representations, with $L(A)'=R(A)$ and
$R(A)'=L(A)$. A vector $\xi \in L^2(A)$ defines a bounded map $a\mapsto \xi a$ on $L^2(A)$
if and only if $\xi $ is represented by an element of $A$. Every positive normal
functional is $a\mapsto \langle a\xi ,\xi \rangle $ for some $\xi \in L^2(A)$. If $D\subseteq A$ is a unital von
Neumann subalgebra, there is a unique normal faithful trace-preserving
conditional expectation $E_D:A\to D$; it is the restriction of the orthogonal
projection onto $L^2(D)$ and is contractive and $D$-bimodular.

Assume AC. In a factor $Q$, any two projections $p,q$ are comparable by subequivalence.
If $Q$ has a faithful normal semifinite trace $s$ and $s(p),s(q)<\infty$, then
$p\precsim q$ if and only if $s(p)\le s(q)$, and equality means equivalence.
Every nonzero corner of a diffuse factor is again a diffuse factor. A diffuse
finite factor has a unique normalized tracial state. Finite matrix
amplifications of a II1 factor and all their nonzero corners are II1 factors.

Assume AC. For a finite tracial algebra $(N,t)$, every Hilbert space $H$ with a normal
unital right $N$ action, meaning a unital star anti-homomorphism into $B(H)$ that is WOT continuous on bounded balls, is right-unitarily isomorphic to
$P(\ell^2(I)\otimes L^2(N))$, where $I$ is an arbitrary set and
$P\in B(\ell^2(I)) \bar\otimes N$ is a projection. Its bounded right-linear operator
algebra is the corner $P(B(\ell^2(I)) \bar\otimes N)P$. The formula
$\operatorname{Tr}_N(T)=\sum _i t(T_{ii})$ for positive $T$ defines a faithful normal
semifinite trace on the ambient algebra and its corner. Transport to $H$
is independent of the model; its value at the identity defines $\dim_N H$.
If $N$ is a II1 factor and this dimension is finite, $H$ is isomorphic to
$p L^2(N)^k$ for some finite $k$ and $p\in M_k(N)$, with
$\dim_N H=(\operatorname{Tr}_k\otimes t)(p)$.

Assume AC. A **II1 factor** is a von Neumann algebra $A$ with center $\mathbb C1$, no nonzero minimal projections, and a faithful normal normalized trace $\tau_A$, with the operator and trace conventions of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]] and [[def-tracial-state-and-faithful-normal-trace-on-a-von-neumann-algebra]]. A **II1 subfactor inclusion** is a unital inclusion $N\subseteq M$ of II1 factors, with $\tau_N=\tau_M|_N$. Its trace-preserving normal faithful conditional expectation $E_N:M\to N$ is the unique expectation constructed in [[lem-tracial-standard-form-and-normal-functional-vectors]]; it is positive, unital, $N$-bimodular, and the restriction of the orthogonal projection $e_N:L^2(M)\to L^2(N)$.

A **normal right Hilbert-space $N$-module** is a Hilbert space with a unital star representation of $N^{\mathrm{op}}$ that is WOT-continuous on the operator-norm unit ball. This is the topological normality convention of the trace definition above. Right multiplication is $R_a(x)=xa$, so $R_aR_b=R_{ba}$. The amplification theorem [[lem-tracial-hilbert-module-dimension-and-finite-corners]] constructs a right-module unitary $H\cong P(\ell^2(I)\otimes L^2(N))$ and its model-independent canonical semifinite trace on $\operatorname{End}_N(H)$, given in that model by $\operatorname{Tr}_H(T)=\sum_{i\in I}\tau_N(T_{ii})$ for positive $T$. Define $\dim_N H=\operatorname{Tr}_H(1)$; in particular $\dim_N L^2(N)=1$. The **ordinary Jones index** of the inclusion is
$$[M:N]=\dim_N L^2(M,\tau_M)=:\lambda.$$
The inclusion has **finite index** when $\lambda<\infty$. No finite bounded frame or complete $N$-valued module model is part of this hypothesis.

For finite index, put $B=\operatorname{End}_N L^2(M)$ and $\tau_B=\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}_{L^2(M)}$. Let $J(x)=x^*$ on $L^2(M)$, so $R_a=JL_{a^*}J$. The inclusion is **extremal** when
$$\tau_B(R_a)=\tau_M(a)\qquad(a\in N'\cap M).$$
Here $N'\cap M=\{a\in M:an=na\text{ for every }n\in N\}$, and $R_a$ belongs to $B$ for these $a$. Equivalently, the normalized trace on the commutant of the left $N$ action and $\tau_M$ agree on $N'\cap M$, transported by $J$. This specifies the right-action trace: the normalized trace of $B$ on the left action of $M$ agrees automatically with $\tau_M$ and does not define extremality.

For later calculations write $\mathcal X=M$ with $N$-valued inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_N=E_N(x^*y)$ and norm $\|x\|_{\mathcal X}=\|E_N(x^*x)\|^{1/2}$. Its completeness, finite projection model $\mathcal X\cong pN^k$, and bounded coordinate frame are consequences proved below from ordinary finite index; they are not additional assumptions. No separability or irreducibility hypothesis is imposed.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$D\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a nondegenerate concrete C*-algebra
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]],
[[def-c-star-algebra]], [[def-nondegenerate-star-representation-of-a-banach-star-algebra]]).
Set $M:=D''$ in the commutant convention of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]]. If $H=\{0\}$, the operator-density and transitivity clauses below
are trivial; assume $H\ne\{0\}$ for those clauses. Then:

1. $D_{\mathrm{sa}}$ is strongly dense in $M_{\mathrm{sa}}$, and the unit ball
   of $D$ is strongly dense in the unit ball of $M$.
2. If $M=\mathcal B(H)$, then every finite self-adjoint vector prescription
   compatible with a self-adjoint operator is realized exactly: for
   $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\in H$ and $c=c^*\in\mathcal B(H)$, there is
   $a=a^*\in D$ with $a\xi_j=c\xi_j$ for all $j$. Separately, if the prescribed vectors are finitely many orthonormal
   eigenvectors of $c$ with eigenvalues in a closed interval
   $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ containing $0$, an $a\in D_{\mathrm{sa}}$ can be
   chosen with spectrum in $J$ and the same eigenvalues on those vectors.
   This spectrum-constrained variant makes no promise about additional
   arbitrary vector prescriptions after clipping.
3. If $M=\mathcal B(H)$, then for any unit vectors $\xi,\eta\in H$ there is a unitary $u$ in the
   minimal unitization $D^\sim$ ([[thm-minimal-c-star-unitization]]) whose
   represented operator sends $\xi$ to $z\eta$ for some $z\in\mathbb C$ with
   $|z|=1$. Here unitary has the usual C*-algebra meaning
   ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-elements-of-a-c-star-algebra]]),
   and $D^\sim=D$ when $D$ is unital and $D+\mathbb C I$ otherwise.

For a complex C*-algebra $A$, two pure states $\phi,\psi$ are called unitarily
equivalent here when $\psi=\phi\circ\operatorname{Ad}(u)$ for some unitary
$u\in U(A^\sim)$, where $\operatorname{Ad}(u)(a)=uau^*$ and $A^\sim=A$ when
$A$ is unital and its minimal unitization otherwise
([[thm-minimal-c-star-unitization]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-elements-of-a-c-star-algebra]]). Their GNS
representations are irreducible exactly when the states are pure
([[lem-c-star-state-gns-purity-and-polish-state-space]],
[[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]]). If their GNS representations are
inequivalent, then $\|\phi-\psi\|=2$. Orthogonal unit vectors in one
irreducible carrier likewise give vector states at distance $2$. Consequently,
if $\|\phi-\psi\|<2$, then $\phi$ and $\psi$ are unitarily equivalent.

**Assume the ultrafilter lemma.**  If $X$ is a real or complex normed space,
then its closed dual unit ball $B_{X^*}$ is compact in the weak-star topology
$\sigma(X^*,X)$.  Completeness of $X$ is not required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital $*$-subalgebra closed in the weak operator topology. Then $M''=M$, and $M$ is also closed in the strong operator topology. Consequently the concrete von Neumann algebras of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]] are exactly the unital $*$-subalgebras that are closed in either of these topologies. For an arbitrary set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ one has $W^*(\mathcal S)''=W^*(\mathcal S)$.

Orthogonal projection gives $exe=E_N(x)e$ directly on the dense subspace $M$, and $Je=eJ$ since $L^2(N)$ is invariant under the conjugation $J$. If an element of $M'$ commutes with $e$, [[lem-tracial-standard-form-and-normal-functional-vectors]] writes it as $R_a$, $a\in M$; applying the commutation equation to $1$ says $a=E_N(a)\in N$. Conversely right $N$ commutes with both $M$ and $e$. Bicommutants therefore give $W^*(M,e)=(R(N))'=B$. [[lem-tracial-hilbert-module-dimension-and-finite-corners]] makes this a finite-trace factor; it is diffuse because it has the diffuse corner $eBe=N e$, or by its finite matrix corner model. To verify the corner assertion independently, restriction of $T\in eBe$ to $L^2(N)$ commutes with right $N$, so is left multiplication by some $n\in N$ by [[lem-tracial-standard-form-and-normal-functional-vectors]]. Hence $T=ne$.

Let $V_x:L^2(N)\to H$ be $n\mapsto xn$. Then $V_x V_y^*=xey^*$ and $V_y^*V_x=E_N(y^*x)$ as a left multiplier on $L^2(N)$. The rectangular trace calculation from [[lem-tracial-hilbert-module-dimension-and-finite-corners]] gives $\operatorname{Tr}_B(xey)=\tau (yx)$ by polarization. In particular $\operatorname{Tr}_B(e)=1$. Its normalized restriction $\lambda ^{-1} \operatorname{Tr}_B|_M$ is a tracial state, hence equals $\tau $ by [[lem-finite-factor-projection-comparison-and-normalized-trace]]. [[lem-tracial-standard-form-and-normal-functional-vectors]] applied to the finite tracial algebra $(B,\lambda ^{-1} \operatorname{Tr}_B)$ gives the expectation $F$. For $a\in M$, $\lambda \tau (aF(e))=\operatorname{Tr}_B(ae)=\tau (a)$. Nondegeneracy of the trace pairing gives $F(e)=\lambda ^{-1} 1$, and bimodularity gives the displayed formula for $F(xey)$.

The *-algebra $A_0=\operatorname{span} MeM$ is strongly dense in $B$. One way to see this with no frame assumption is that its WOT closure is a two-sided ideal of $B$ and contains $e$. Finite trace comparison gives finitely many orthogonal projections summing to $1$, each subequivalent to $e$: remove copies of $e$ while the remainder has trace greater than $1$, then embed the last remainder in $e$. If $v_j$ are the resulting partial isometries, $1=\sum_jv_j e v_j^*$ belongs to this ideal, so the ideal is all of $B$. Applying [F8] to the nondegenerate C*-closure of $A_0$ gives, for each $T\in B$, a net $a_i\in A_0$ converging strongly to $T$ with a common operator bound (apply it first to the C*-closure of $A_0$, then approximate each resulting bounded element in norm by $A_0$, allowing a fixed arbitrarily small bound slack). Writing $a_i=\sum  x_r e y_r$ gives $a_i e=x_i e$, where $x_i=\sum  x_r E_N(y_r)\in M$. The expectation formula shows $x_i=\lambda F(a_i e)$ and $\|x_i\|\le \lambda \|a_i\|$. A bounded subnet has an ultraweak limit $x\in M$; the matrix coefficients of left multiplication on $L^2(M)$ are normal, so $x_i e\to xe$ weakly. But $a_i e\to Te$ strongly, thus $Te=xe$. Applying $F$ to this identity gives $x=\lambda F(Te)$; uniqueness also follows by applying $xe$ to $1$. This proof does not silently pass an unbounded inverse through a weak limit.

If $\xi $ is right-$N$ bounded, its bounded map $V_\xi :L^2(N)\to H$ extends by zero on $L^2(N)^\perp$ to $T=V_\xi  e\in B$. Pull-down gives $T=xe$, so $\xi =T1=x$. This proves equality of the right-$N$ bounded vectors and $M$.

$$u_i u_{i+1}u_i-u_i,\qquad u_{i+1}u_i u_{i+1}-u_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2).$$

$$P_n(R,\delta):=F_n/I_n.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. If $m+n$ is odd, there are no such diagrams. Write $\mathcal D(m,n)$ for this set and define the $R$-module

$$M_R(m,n):=R^{(\mathcal D(m,n))},$$

the free $R$-module on the set of diagrams ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). In particular, its diagram basis is empty when $m+n$ is odd.

For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. Denote this output by $E\circ D$ and extend the rule $R$-bilinearly to a map $M_R(n,p)\times M_R(m,n)\to M_R(m,p)$. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

The matching $1_n:n\to n$ pairs each bottom point to the top point directly above it. Horizontal juxtaposition, with the left diagram placed first, defines $m\otimes m'=m+m'$ on object labels and $D\otimes D'$ on basis diagrams; extend it $R$-bilinearly to the modules. A following result proves that these operations give a strict monoidal category.

For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in M_R(n,n)$ be the diagram with a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at every other position.
